sources.title: Split-thickness skin graft donor-site morbidity: a systematic literature review

sources.org: Brown JE et al. Int Wound J 15:1000
sources.title: An evidence-based review of split-thickness skin graft donor site dressings

indications: Wounds with a vascular bed that cannot be closed directly: granulating wounds, fasciotomy wounds, debrided burns and areas of skin loss.
Temporary or definitive cover where a flap is not required.
contraindications: A bed without blood supply: bare cortical bone without periosteum, tendon without paratenon, cartilage without perichondrium, or exposed metalwork. These need a flap.
Active infection of the bed, particularly beta-haemolytic streptococci, which destroy grafts.
preparation: A clean, granulating or freshly debrided bed with controlled bioburden.
Choose the donor site with the patient: the thigh is common; consider colour match for the face and visibility of the scar.
Consent covers graft loss, donor site pain and healing, scarring, pigment change and contracture.
positioning: Positioned so both donor and recipient sites are accessible, with pressure areas protected.
equipment: Powered or hand dermatome, mesher and carriers.
Staples, absorbable sutures or tissue glue for fixation.
Bolster or negative-pressure dressing; donor site dressing.
anatomy: A split-thickness graft carries epidermis and part of the dermis; the donor heals from adnexal remnants in the remaining dermis.
Thinner grafts take more reliably and the donor heals faster; thicker grafts contract less and look better.
Graft take proceeds through plasmatic imbibition, then inosculation and revascularisation, so intimate contact with the bed is essential.
criticalSafety: Prepare the bed before harvesting the graft: a perfect graft on a poor bed fails.
Dermis side down. A graft placed upside down will not take.
Prevent shear, haematoma and seroma: these, with infection, account for most graft loss.
structuresAtRisk: Donor site (excess depth produces a full-thickness wound)
Exposed tendon, bone or vessels in the recipient bed
commonErrors: Harvesting too deep, converting the donor into a slow-healing wound.
Poor immobilisation over a joint, so the graft shears.
complications: Partial or complete graft loss from haematoma, seroma, shear or infection.
Donor site pain, delayed healing, hypertrophic scarring and pigment change.
postop: Immobilise and elevate the grafted area; splint across joints.
First graft inspection at a planned interval set by the surgeon, earlier if there is pain, odour or discharge.
Moist wound healing dressings on the donor site, left undisturbed unless they leak or the wound looks infected.
Moisturise and protect the healed graft from sun.

steps.emphasis: Both donor and recipient sites accessible without repositioning. Protect heels and sacrum in a long case.
On a limb recipient site, inflate only for bed preparation and deflate for haemostasis before the graft goes on.
Excise granulation tissue and slough to a flat, bleeding, healthy bed.
Haemostasis of the bed is graft survival. Any haematoma lifts the graft off its blood supply.
Document graft source, size, meshing ratio, fixation and the date of first inspection.

step.stsg.harvest.title: Graft harvest
step.stsg.harvest.why: The depth of harvest decides both whether the graft takes and how well the donor heals. A uniform, thin graft serves both.
how: Mark the area required; lubricate the donor and keep the skin under tension.
Set the dermatome depth and width, and check them before cutting.
Harvest with steady pressure at a constant angle. Fine, dense punctate bleeding in the donor indicates a thin split graft; sparse larger points mean a deeper cut.
pitfalls: An uneven graft from inconsistent pressure.

step.stsg.mesh.title: Meshing or fenestration
step.stsg.mesh.why: Meshing lets blood and serum escape and expands the graft. It also leaves a pattern, so it is a decision about appearance as well as take.
how: Mesh at the ratio the wound needs, or fenestrate with a blade for sheet grafts.
Use unmeshed sheet graft on the face and hands where appearance and contracture matter most.
Keep the graft moist and identify the dermal side before transfer.
pitfalls: Over-expanding a mesh so that interstices heal slowly.
Losing track of which side is dermis.

step.stsg.inset.title: Graft inset and fixation
step.stsg.inset.why: A graft takes only where it touches a vascular bed and stays still. Inset is about contact and immobility.
how: Lay the graft dermal side down on the bed with slight tension, avoiding folds.
Fix the edges with staples, sutures or glue, trimming the excess.
Express blood or serum from beneath before dressing.

step.stsg.dressing.title: Graft dressing and immobilisation
step.stsg.dressing.why: Shear and fluid collections are the commonest preventable causes of graft loss; the dressing exists to stop both.
how: Use a non-adherent contact layer then a bolster tie-over or a negative-pressure dressing.
Splint across any joint the graft crosses.
Record the planned date of first inspection.
pitfalls: A bulky dressing without even pressure.

step.stsg.donor.title: Donor site dressing
step.stsg.donor.why: Donor site pain often troubles patients more than the recipient site. Dressing choice changes pain and healing time.
how: Apply a moist wound-healing dressing per local formulary; evidence favours moist dressings over dry gauze for pain and healing.
Consider local anaesthetic infiltration or topical agents for donor pain.
Leave the dressing undisturbed unless it leaks or the site looks infected.
pitfalls: Dry gauze adhering to the healing donor.
Frequent changes that strip new epithelium.
